history_of_present_illness: Liver abscess was first noted by Hippocrates who described a method for its evacuation. The understanding of its connection to amoebae in liver abscesses is more recent (1887) and linked to the history of amoebic dysentery. The disease typically follows a case of amoebic dysentery, either during convalescence or later. Patients experience an irregular fever with an evening rise and profuse, often colliquative sweats. A marked feeling of weight in the liver region progresses to tenderness or pain upon palpation. Pain may be referred to the right shoulder (for upper convex abscesses) or the appendix region (for inferior concave abscesses). Abscesses in the left lobe can present with gastric symptoms. Patients tend to splint the liver, often lying on their right side or holding their right arm to their side, and may exhibit rigidity of the right rectus muscle. Respiratory symptoms include moist crepitation at the right lung base, a dry cough (tussis hepatica), and shallow respirations due to pain on deep inspiration. Insomnia is common, and while jaundice is rare, an earthy or subicteroid skin tinging may be noted. The urine is scanty, high-colored, with increased ammonia nitrogen and urobilin. Some cases may present with practically no symptoms.
exposure_and_epidemiology: The geographical distribution of liver abscess is closely related to the prevalence of amoebic dysentery, particularly in tropical centers where white men may lack knowledge of health maintenance. Historically, it was common in the Philippines following American occupation but has since become rare in Americans due to education and more temperate living. The exciting cause is *Entamoeba histolytica*, which travels from amoebic intestinal ulcerations, plugging portal capillaries and causing gelatinous necrosis in the liver. A history of amoebic dysentery is obtained in 60-90% of liver abscess cases, though amoebic lesions may be found at autopsy in individuals who never showed dysentery symptoms. Amoebic liver abscess is exceedingly rare in children and about 10 times less common in women than men. Intemperance and abuse of alcohol are significant predisposing factors, noted in 67.5% of cases by Waring. Natives of India rarely develop liver abscess unless they adopt European eating and drinking customs. Approximately 20% of amoebic dysentery cases are complicated by liver abscess. The abscess can manifest years after a patient has left the tropics or after any dysenteric symptoms have occurred, even without demonstrable intestinal lesions (which may have healed or been microscopic).
vitals: A rather irregular type of fever is noted, which shows an evening rise with sweatings. The morning temperature is frequently normal, and there may be frequent apyretic intervals. A low remittent fever is present in the pre-suppurative stage.
physical_exam: The liver shows a marked feeling of weight, which may later develop into tenderness or pain upon palpation. The right side of the liver typically enlarges in an upward direction, which can be measured with a tape-measure and confirmed by X-rays. Pain may be referred to the right shoulder (when the abscess is in the upper convex part of the liver) or the region of the appendix (when nearer the inferior concave surface). There is a marked tendency to splint the liver, causing the patient to lie towards the right side and apply their right arm to their side when walking. The right rectus often shows rigidity. Auscultation of the base of the right lung reveals moist crepitation. There is rarely any jaundice, but an earthy color or subicteroid tinging is often noted. Superficial veins may be enlarged. The spleen typically shows no enlargement.
labs_and_diagnostics: Diagnosis involves a history of previous dysentery, hectic fever, crepitation at the right lung base, pain, and upward enlargement of the liver. X-ray imaging is valuable for confirming upward liver enlargement, which can be as high as the angle of the scapula, differentiating it from most other conditions that cause downward enlargement. The amelioration of symptoms after two to three days of subcutaneous emetine administration is diagnostically significant. Laboratory findings include a constant but low leucocytosis (12,000 to 20,000) with approximately 70% polymorphonuclears and an increase in large mononuclears to 10-15%. The final proof is obtaining characteristic chocolate-colored or anchovy sauce-like pus via exploratory puncture. This pus, if not bacterially contaminated, lacks polymorphonuclears and initially does not show amoebae (they appear around the third day from the drainage tube), but may contain granular débris, cholesterin, and haematoidin crystals. Schilling-Torgau's modification of Arneth's index can reveal a displacement to the left in the differential count (presence of immature polymorphonuclears like band-forms or myelocytes), indicating liver abscess even with a normal total white count, and can suggest prognosis. Iodophilia may be found. Functional liver tests include determining the ammonia quotient (increased nitrogen eliminated as ammonia) and the lipase test. The urobilinogen test, using Ehrlich's aldehyde reagent (producing a cherry-red color), is considered the most specific test for hepatic function disturbances.
differential_diagnosis: Syphilitic gummata (differentiated by irregular, downward enlargement and response to iodide of potash), suppurative pylephlebitis (often with jaundice, from colon/appendix infections), pyaemic (multiple) abscesses of the liver (often with jaundice), suppurative cholangitis and cholecystitis (history of biliary colic, jaundice, tenderness at ninth rib tip, gall bladder tumor), empyema (history of pleurisy or pneumonia), suppurating hydatid cyst (differentiated by echinococcus hooklets or complement fixation test), tuberculosis (especially when abscess ruptures into lungs), malaria, abscess in the kidney or perinephritic region. An abscess of the abdominal wall can be differentiated by the exploring needle not moving with respiration, unlike a liver abscess.
management_and_clinical_course: Prophylaxis is similar to that for amoebic dysentery, emphasizing avoidance of factors that reduce liver function, such as overfeeding and alcoholic excesses. Given that abscesses can occur months or years after an acute amoebic dysentery attack, a preventive measure suggested is to administer one grain of emetine on two or three successive days each month following an acute attack. For the pre-suppurative stage of amoebic hepatitis, treatment with emetine or ipecac can lead to a cure and prevent abscess formation. Once an abscess forms, treatment is primarily surgical and should be instituted immediately upon diagnosis. Earlier drainage improves patient recovery, speeds convalescence, and yields a better prognosis. The trocar and cannula method, once condemned, is now considered by some to be sufficient with the advent of emetine, potentially avoiding more radical operations. This procedure involves aspirating with a needle to locate pus, then introducing a trocar and cannula, followed by rubber drainage tubing. Aspiration alone or aspiration with the injection of 1:1000 emetine solution or quinine irrigations into the cavity have also been reported. While subcutaneous emetine has shown promise, including reports of cure without operation, recent experience indicates that evacuation of pus is generally necessary. Surgical approaches include vertical or Kocher incisions for abdominal access, with transpleural routes preferred for abscesses located far back or high up in the liver, sometimes involving rib resection. Newman warned against using a small aspirator for diagnosis due to unreliability and risks like internal hemorrhage and peritoneal infection, recommending incision and packing with gauze, and exploration with dressing forceps rather than a knife.
